comparison: Both evaluate the successful differentiation and characterization of cell types (C1, C2, C6). OpenEval emphasizes canonical markers and sequencing depth (C89, C90), while peer reviewers focus on methodological approach and data quality. Both find the evidence SUPPORTED, though peer reviewers note the limitation of using only two iPSC clones.

Both address clustering analyses (C3, C4, C5). OpenEval highlights the importance of line-to-line variability control, while peer reviewers incorporate these claims into their broader endorsement of the study's methodological approach. Both find evidence SUPPORTED.

Both evaluate the identification of ASE genes with cell-type-specific patterns (C7, C8, C53). OpenEval emphasizes the thousands of ASE genes identified, while peer reviewers explicitly endorse this as a primary finding with 'convincing evidence.' Both find evidence SUPPORTED, with peer reviewers also including C68 in their evaluation.

Both assess the enrichment of ASE in cell-type-specific genes (C10-C14, C54). OpenEval emphasizes extensive robustness checks and constraint stratification, while peer reviewers accept the finding without challenge and note the conclusion about positive selection. Both find evidence SUPPORTED, with peer reviewers also including C55 in their evaluation.

Perfect overlap on claims C15-C23, C56, C69, C99 regarding lineage-specific selection. Both find evidence SUPPORTED and highlight functionally relevant pathways. OpenEval notes the lack of electrophysiology data (C118) as a limitation, while peer reviewers explicitly highlight this as a key finding in their abstract.

Both address ATAC-seq data generation and quality (C24-C27). OpenEval notes a minor peak count discrepancy (C100), while peer reviewers accept the ATAC-seq findings and include the heterochromatin observations (C28-C33) in their evaluation. Both find evidence SUPPORTED.

Both evaluate heterochromatin findings (C29-C33). OpenEval emphasizes the unexpected nature of the finding and the distinction between proximal and distal regions, while peer reviewers accept it as an observation without critique. Both find evidence SUPPORTED.

Perfect overlap on claims C34-C37 regarding ASCA enrichment in cell-type-specific peaks. Both emphasize robustness checks and find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval details down-sampling analysis and SNP stratification, while peer reviewers affirm this as part of the primary conclusions with 'convincing evidence.'

Both evaluate novel metrics for concordance between ASE and ASCA (C38, C39, C57, C58). OpenEval finds evidence SUPPORTED and notes the 'neither necessary nor sufficient' interpretation (C108), while peer reviewers also find it SUPPORTED and accept the methodological contribution without concerns.

Perfect overlap on FABP7 case study claims (C40-C44, C59-C60, C109-C110, C121). OpenEval finds evidence SUPPORTED but notes functional consequences remain speculative. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, explicitly stating 'the described variants lack any functional validation' and emphasizing the need for additional work to demonstrate functionality.

Perfect overlap on GAD1 case study claims (C45-C52, C61-C62, C111-C115, C122-C123). OpenEval finds evidence SUPPORTED with strong converging evidence but acknowledges uncertainty about functional consequences. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN with the same concerns as FABP7, noting lack of functional validation and that authors 'have opted to defer these validations to future studies.'

Both address quality control issues (C92, C93). OpenEval emphasizes the simulation-based validation and transparency, finding evidence SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers include these claims in their broader evaluation of experimental design and acknowledge the contamination correction without challenge, also finding evidence SUPPORTED.

Both evaluate SKM data limitations (C94, C95). OpenEval finds the robustness check appropriate and evidence SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers include this in their evaluation of experimental design, noting the limitation of two iPSC clones but accepting the authors' handling of data quality issues.

Perfect overlap on neurotrophin family examples (C9, C96, C97). Both find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes this as an effective illustration of cell-type-specific divergence complexity, while peer reviewers accept these as supporting evidence for the broader finding without challenge.

Both address interpretations about selection versus constraint (C55, C116, C117). OpenEval finds the cautious interpretation SUPPORTED and consistent with data. Peer reviewers also find it SUPPORTED, noting the authors acknowledge 'it remains unclear whether positive selection or lower constraint plays a larger role' and accepting this honest assessment.

Perfect overlap on background and context claims (C63-C88). Both find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes these accurately represent the field and are well-cited, while peer reviewers affirm the study's conceptual framework and methodological approach, particularly endorsing the hybrid cell advantages.

Both address the hybrid cell approach advantage (C98). OpenEval includes this with methods and limitations, finding it SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers explicitly endorse the value of the hybrid cell approach for differentiating cis-regulatory from trans effects, also finding it SUPPORTED.

Both evaluate limitations and uncertainties (C118, C119). OpenEval includes these with methods and future directions, finding the acknowledgments appropriate and SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers accept these limitations without challenge, also finding them SUPPORTED.

Perfect overlap on future directions (C124-C126). Both find these SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes they are reasonable extensions of the work, while peer reviewers implicitly support them by noting current limitations that align with the proposed future work.

Both address heterochromatin interpretations (C103, C104). OpenEval finds these interpretations consistent with data and SUPPORTED, emphasizing the distinction between proximal and distal regions. Peer reviewers accept these technical details and interpretations without challenge, also finding them SUPPORTED.

Both address the 'neither necessary nor sufficient' interpretation (C108). OpenEval includes this with the novel metrics evaluation, finding it appropriately acknowledges regulatory complexity and is SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers accept this nuanced interpretation, implicitly supporting it by noting the limited number of concordant CRE-gene pairs.

Both address experimental design elements (C89, C90). OpenEval includes these in the differentiation success evaluation, finding them SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers note the limitation of only two iPSC clones and emphasize the need for more replicates, but still find the evidence SUPPORTED.

Both reference ATAC-seq peak counts (C100). OpenEval notes a minor discrepancy between C25 and C100, finding it likely reflects different filtering stages and is SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers include this in their acceptance of ATAC-seq technical details without challenge.
